column11: Chagigah 15b: ‘When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael to Babylonia, he said: In the West, Eretz Yisrael, they say: Rabbi Meir ate a half-ripe date and threw the peel away. column11: Berakhot 57b: ‘The numbers five, six, and ten are mnemonics for the categories to follow. The Gemara says: There are five matters in our world which are one-sixtieth of their most extreme manifestations. They are: Fire, honey, Shabbat, sleep, and a dream. The Gemara elaborates: Our fire is one-sixtieth of the fire of Gehenna; honey is one-sixtieth of manna; Shabbat is one-sixtieth of the World-to-Come; sleep is one-sixtieth of death; and a dream is one-sixtieth of prophecy.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Kislev 2, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 57b) to illuminate his exposition here (“For sleep, it states in the Gemara (Berachot 57b), is one-sixtieth of death, – and in the Midrash Rabbah there the phrasing is: "The unripe fruit of death is sleep". And it states in holy books:...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And this is termed the World to Come because then this vital pulse will be tangibly felt; whereas currently "when Hashem turned again the captivity... we were like unto them that dream", as in sleep where one does not feel his vitality, sleep being one-sixtieth of death (Berakhot 57b), yet not actual death. Likewise in the Gemara the death of the righteous is termed demakh (sleep), for literal death applies only to the wicked who "even in their lifetime are called dead", possessing no divine vitality; whereas "Thy people are all righteous", cleaving to their concealed root in Hashem whence vitality flows to the heart, so that all possess vitality.

column11: Zohar, Toldot 15:119-16:128: ‘A man, therefore, should not confidently affirm: “God will deliver me or will do for me this or that”; but he should endeavour to fulfil the precepts of the Law and to walk in the path of truth, and then put his full trust in Him that He will help him thereto. For assuredly whenever a man sets out to purify himself he is helped thereto from on high. A man should thus put his trust in God and not anywhere else. Hence the expression “whose strength is in thee”. The next words, “in whose heart are paths”, indicate that a man should purge his heart of all strange thoughts, so as to make it like a path that leads straight to the desired destination.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Kislev 2, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Toldot 15:119-16:128) to illuminate his exposition here (“concerning which Israel holds bold confidence, as written in the Holy Zohar (Part I, 142a) on the verse: "Whose strength is in You, in whose heart are the highways, see there"; if he will only...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.

column11: Berakhot 61b: ‘We learned in our mishna the explanation of the verse: “And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and all your soul and all your might” (Deuteronomy 6:5). This was elaborated upon when it was taught in a baraita: Rabbi Eliezer says: If it is stated: “With all your soul,” why does it state: “With all your might”? Conversely, if it stated: “With all your might,” why does it state: “With all your soul”? Rather, this means that if one’s body is dearer to him than his property, therefore it is stated: “With all your soul”; one must give his soul in sanctification of God. And if one’s money is dearer to him than his body, therefore it is stated: “With all your might”; with all…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Kislev 3, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 61b) to illuminate his exposition here (“which accords with what is written in the Gemara (Berachot 61b): "The stomach sleeps." column11: Nedarim 15a: ‘Rather, it is obvious that the mishna is referring to a case where one said: Sleeping is konam to my eyes today if I sleep tomorrow. column13: Section 14: Mordechai's Five Royal Garments Matching the Five Soul-Levels, Shatnez in the Girdle, and Transforming Evil on Purim The theme: The five royal garments of Mordechai corresponding to the five soul-dimensions (Naran-Chai), the linen and wool girdle reconciling the two inclinations, and Purim sweetening the bitter into "very good". Scripture enumerates five royal items for Mordechai: blue (techelet), white (chur), a crown of gold (ateret zahav), fine linen (butz), and purple wool (argaman) (Esther 8:15). These correspond to the five levels of the soul: Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah, Chayah, and Yechidah.

column11: Megillah 16b: ‘The next line of the song inverts the sequence. This is the principle for all songs in the Bible except for this song, referring to the list of Haman’s sons, and the song listing the kings of Canaan who were defeated by Joshua. These two songs are written in the form of a half brick arranged upon a half brick and a whole brick arranged upon a whole brick, i.e., one stitch of text over another, and one blank space over another. What is the reason that these two songs are written in this anomalous fashion? So that they should never rise from their downfall. Just as a wall that is built in this manner will not stand, so too, these individuals should have no resurgence.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 1, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Megillah 16b) to illuminate his exposition here (“And so they expounded: "'And honor (yekar)' — these are the tefillin of the head" (Megillah 16b), which means that yekar points to the Supreme Crown (Keter Elyon) as we have stated many times.”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.

column11: Zohar, Terumah 76:742-77:751: ‘Concerning the mystery of the light which kindles and produces the light in the lamp, it was said unto Aaron: “When thou lightest the lamps” (Num. 8, 2); for he emanated from the region of that light. Concerning this, too, it is written: “Let there be light, and there was light” (Gen. 1, 3). Why, it may be asked, was it necessary to repeat the word “light” in this verse? The answer is that the first “light” refers to the primordial light which is of the Right Hand, and is destined for the “end of days”; while the second “light” refers to the Left Hand, which issues from the Right.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 1, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Terumah 76:742-77:751) to illuminate his exposition here (“And in the Holy Zohar (Part II, 167a) that "and there was light" indicates the light of the Oral Torah, which matches what is written in the Tikunim (Tikun 21): "From the right was given the...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And there revealed the very summit of his knowledge in saying that he had no [full] resolution for it, “for our knowing is not like His knowing” — and that [very admission] is the true resolution of this difficulty, and not as the Ra’avad [charged], that he “left it as a difficulty.”.” R’ Tzadok defends the Rambam against the charge: far from leaving it unresolved, the Rambam disclosed “the very summit of his knowledge” in recognizing that the human intellect cannot apprehend how God’s foreknowledge and man’s free choice cohere — and that recognition is the answer itself, “for our knowing is not like His knowing.”

column15: As stated in the Holy Zohar (Noach 74a): Come and see: concerning Nimrod what is written? ‘And the beginning of his kingdom was Babel’—for from there he took hold to bind himself to an alien domain; and likewise: ‘And they found a plain in the land of Shinar.’”

column11: Tikkunei Zohar 42b:2-63a:9: ‘(Ruth 3:13) ... as Y”Y lives lie down until the morning, which is the right-side, in which is the power of the Written Torah, which is the Middle Pillar, for the Written Torah is given from the right-side, and from the left-side is given the Oral Torah, which is ‘female’. And because of this ‘good’, the Righteous-One, ‘the life-force of the worlds’, is from the left-hand side, for it is ‘the mighty-one who conquers his evil inclination’ – which is Samael.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 1, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Tikkunei Zohar 42b:2-63a:9) to illuminate his exposition here (“which matches what is written in the Tikunim (Tikun 21): "From the right was given the Written Torah, and from the left was given the Oral Torah", and so he wrote in the introduction (heading...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: Therefore they count the Flood from Nisan. According to their understanding, even under strict justice there could have been no alternative to the Flood, for sin necessarily draws punishment after it. They believe that a being cannot truly change from what it is. Thus Balaam did not change even though he knew that his path represented the ultimate evil.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 1:23
column15: And this was derived from his being continually attached unto the Life of the Worlds, therefore he was perpetually fervent and swift; and any entity that clings to the Life of the Worlds will never grow stale nor moulder forever. For all deterioration and corruption arise from an entity being detached from the Giver, and deemed as an independent creation in its own right, until it imagines that the might of its own hand 'waxed old, yea, grew mighty in power' (Job 21:7).
